lessons.title: Wie fühlst du dich? Feelings and sich fühlen
lessons.goal: Say how you feel, ask others how they feel and give a reason, using sich fühlen and the reflexive pronouns.

grammar.point: A reflexive pronoun points back to the subject: ich mich, du dich, er/sie/es sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie/Sie sich. Sich fühlen always needs it. In a main clause it stands right after the verb (after a pronoun subject in inversion), in a weil or dass clause right after the subject.
grammar.oneLine: Ich fühle mich gut. Mich points back to ich.

mistake.why: Fühlen needs the reflexive pronoun when you say how you feel: ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, er fühlt sich. Without it, the sentence is not finished.

terms.meaning: the little word (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch) that points back to the subject
a verb used with a reflexive pronoun, written with sich in the dictionary: sich fühlen
the person or thing that does the verb: Mira in Mira fühlt sich gut

cards.title: Before we start: how are you, really?
cards.body: Welcome to chapter 4, Große und kleine Gefühle. The WG has good days, bad moods and a few quarrels, and you learn to talk about all of it. You already say Mir geht es gut and Ich bin müde. Today you add one small word that makes feelings sound natural: Ich fühle mich gut.
steps: You already know: Mir geht es gut, Ich bin müde, and mich and dich from A1 (Ben sieht mich).
New today: the reflexive pronoun, the little word mich that points back to ich.
By the end you can: say how you feel, ask others how they feel and give a reason.

examples.why: You know this already: mich is another person here.
New today. Card 2 gives mich in this sentence its own colour.

cards.more: Think of a mirror. In Ben sieht mich, Ben looks at me, and I am a different person. In Ich fühle mich gut, the feeling goes from me back to me, like looking in the mirror. English hides this little word (I feel good), but German says it out loud: ich fühle mich. The next cards go slowly: first more feeling words, then the little word itself, then every person, questions, feeling nouns and reasons.

cards.title: Feelings: four new words for how you are
cards.body: You know froh, traurig, wütend and nervös. Four more: glücklich (happy), stolz (proud), erleichtert (relieved) and überrascht (surprised). After sein they never change: Ich bin glücklich. Mira ist erleichtert. Each one fits a situation, so link the word to a small picture.
cards.lead: The introduction showed Ich fühle mich gut. First you need the feeling words themselves, so that you can say more than gut and müde.

deeper.text: Stolz can say who or what you are proud of: stolz auf plus accusative. For now learn it as a block, because it fits one sentence you will want soon. The little word dich here is the normal accusative pronoun from A1, not a reflexive one, because you are proud of another person.

example.de: Ich bin stolz auf dich.
example.en: I am proud of you.

cards.more: Each feeling is a small picture. Happy is a big smile on a good day. Proud is standing tall after you did something well. Relieved is the breath you let out when something scary is over. Surprised is wide eyes when something you did not expect happens. After sein the word stays the same for everybody, so you learn it only once.

rows: a big smile, a good day

cards.title: Ich fühle mich gut: the person does it to themselves
cards.body: In Ben sieht mich, mich is another person: I am the object. In Ich fühle mich gut, mich means the same person as ich: myself. This little word is a reflexive pronoun, and from now on it has its own colour in the examples. A verb that needs it is a reflexive verb: sich fühlen.
cards.lead: You know the feeling words now. Next comes the small word that German puts between fühle and the feeling: mich. Its new colour shows you when a person does something to themselves.

examples.why: Another person: mich is an object.

deeper.text: In the dictionary a reflexive verb is written with sich in front: sich fühlen. That sich is a reminder: do not learn the verb alone, learn it together with its little word. English often has no word here, so it feels strange at first. Listen for it in every sentence: Ich fühle mich wütend, Ich fühle mich einsam.

example.de: Ich fühle mich wütend.
example.en: I feel angry.

cards.more: Ask one question: who does it, and who gets it? In Ben sieht mich, Ben does it and I get it, two different people, so mich is just an object. In Ich fühle mich gut, I do it and I get it, the same person. When it is the same person, mich is reflexive. Look for the new colour and say: it points back to the subject.
steps: Step 1: find the subject: Ich.
Step 2: find the little word: mich. Does it mean the same person as the subject?
Yes: it is reflexive and gets the new colour. No: it is an ordinary object.

cards.title: Every person: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch
cards.body: The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject. Only one form is new: sich, for er, sie, es, sie (they) and Sie (you, polite). The others you know from A1: mich, dich, uns, euch. Learn the verb in a row: ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, er fühlt sich.
cards.lead: You saw mich with ich. Now you meet all the people, so that you can talk about yourself, a friend, the WG and a group.

deeper.text: Sie with a capital S (you, polite) and sie (they) both use sich, and sich is always written with a small s, even after polite Sie. Only the third person is different: sich fits one person or many, a man, a woman, a thing or a group. That is easier than English, which changes himself, herself, themselves.

example.de: Sie fühlen sich müde.
example.en: They feel tired. / You feel tired (polite).

cards.more: Pretend the pronoun is a shadow that always follows its person. The shadow of ich is mich, of du is dich, of wir is uns, of ihr is euch. For all the others (he, she, it, they and polite you) the shadow looks the same: sich. A common slip is Er fühlt ihn gut. Ihn means a different man, so it sounds wrong. Say Er fühlt sich gut.

cards.title: Ask how somebody feels
cards.body: To ask, put the verb first, then the subject, then the pronoun: Wie fühlst du dich? Fühlt ihr euch wohl? With a name, the pronoun comes first: Wie fühlt sich Ben heute? Fühlst du dich wohl? is a fixed block you can use now: it means Do you feel comfortable?
cards.lead: You can say how everybody feels. Now you learn the same pattern in questions and after a time word, which is how you really talk in the WG.

deeper.text: Notice the order: after a pronoun the reflexive pronoun follows the pronoun (fühle ich mich, fühlst du dich), but before a name it comes first (fühlt sich Ben). It always stays close to the verb. You will not need other positions for a long time, and the same idea works for every subject.

example.de: Wie fühlt sich Ben heute?
example.en: How does Ben feel today?

cards.more: Think of two people standing in a queue behind the verb. If the first person is a short word like du, the pronoun stands behind it: fühlst du dich. If the first person is a long name like Ben or Mira, the little word steps in front: fühlt sich Ben. Either way the pronoun stays right next to the verb, so it is hard to lose.

cards.title: Feelings as nouns: Freude, Angst, Laune, Stimmung
cards.body: Feelings are also nouns: das Gefühl (feeling), die Freude (joy), die Angst (fear), die Laune (mood), die Stimmung (atmosphere). Three blocks to learn whole: Ich habe Angst. Ben hat gute Laune. Die Stimmung ist super. Laune is a short, personal mood; Stimmung is the mood in a group.
cards.lead: Verbs and adjectives let you say how you feel. Nouns let you talk about the feeling itself and about the mood of a room.

examples.en: Ben is in a good mood.

deeper.text: After haben in these blocks there is no article: Ich habe Angst, like Ich habe Hunger. The ending in gute Laune is not explained yet: learn gute Laune and schlechte Laune as two blocks now, and chapter 5 will explain why they end in -e. They also work with another subject: Leon hat schlechte Laune.

example.de: Leon hat schlechte Laune.
example.en: Leon is in a bad mood.

cards.more: Laune is how one person feels today, like the weather inside. Stimmung is the weather in a room: a party has a great Stimmung. Gefühl is the general word. You do not say Ich bin Angst, you say Ich habe Angst, because in German fear is something you have. Learn each noun with its article: das Gefühl, die Freude, die Angst, die Laune, die Stimmung.

cards.title: Give a reason: weil and dass with feelings
cards.body: You know weil and dass: the verb goes to the end. The reflexive pronoun stays close to its subject, directly behind it: Ich fühle mich gut, weil ich Urlaub habe. Mira bleibt zu Hause, weil sie sich müde fühlt. Ich glaube, dass Leon sich einsam fühlt.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer about feelings. The last card shows how to say why, and how to talk about what you believe about someone else.

examples.de: Ich fühle mich gut, weil ich Urlaub habe.
examples.en: I feel good because I am on holiday.

examples.de: Mira bleibt zu Hause, weil sie sich müde fühlt.
examples.en: Mira stays at home because she feels tired.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Leon sich einsam fühlt.
examples.en: I think that Leon feels lonely.

deeper.text: In a clause with weil or dass the pronoun comes right after the subject and before the rest: weil ich mich heute gut fühle. Time words and places come after the pronoun. Even with a name the order is the same: dass Ben sich heute gut fühlt. This is the only place where the pronoun does not stand next to the verb.

example.de: Ich glaube, dass Ben sich heute gut fühlt.
example.en: I think that Ben feels good today.

cards.more: In a weil or dass clause the verb jumps to the end, but the little word does not jump with it. It stays right behind the subject, like a shadow. First the subject, then mich, dich or sich, then everything else, and the verb last. Say weil ich mich müde fühle in your head three times, and the order will feel normal.
steps: Step 1: the main clause, then a comma.
Step 2: weil or dass, then the subject, then the reflexive pronoun.
Step 3: the rest of the clause, with the verb at the end.

lessons.title: Ich freue mich! The common reflexive verbs
lessons.goal: Talk about joy, anger, rest and boredom with everyday reflexive verbs, and say what you look forward to or are happy about.

grammar.point: Many everyday verbs take a reflexive pronoun: sich freuen, sich ärgern, sich aufregen, sich beeilen, sich entspannen. With sich freuen use auf for something ahead and über for something already here or past, both with the accusative. A separable reflexive verb keeps the pronoun right after the verb: Ich rege mich auf.
grammar.oneLine: Ich freue mich auf das Fest. Auf = ahead, über = here or past.

mistake.wrong: Ich freue mich über das Wochenende.
mistake.right: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
mistake.why: The weekend is still ahead, so German uses auf. Use über only for something that is already here or has already happened, like a gift or a message.

terms.meaning: a verb used with mich, dich, sich, uns or euch, listed with sich in the dictionary
a verb whose prefix goes to the end of the sentence: ich rege mich auf
a small word like auf, über or in that goes in front of a noun

cards.title: Before we start: one pattern, many verbs
cards.body: Yesterday you learned Ich fühle mich gut. Today you learn that this is not a single sentence but a pattern: the person does something to themselves, and the verb takes mich, dich or sich. A whole group of everyday verbs works like this, for example freuen, ärgern and entspannen. Learn one pattern, get ten verbs.
steps: You already know: Ich fühle mich gut, and mich, dich, sich, uns, euch.
New today: ten more verbs with the same pattern, and auf and über after sich freuen.
By the end you can: say you are happy, annoyed, bored, relaxed or in a hurry.
cards.more: Imagine a coat with one button hole. The button is the little word mich. Fühlen fits the button, freuen fits it too, and so do ärgern, beeilen and many more. You do not need a new rule for each verb. You only need to remember that these verbs come with their button. The next cards sort the verbs into small groups: joy and anger, calm and stress, boredom and surprise, love, and verbs that can go both ways.

cards.title: Joy and anger: sich freuen, sich ärgern, sich aufregen
cards.body: Three verbs for strong feelings: sich freuen (to be happy), sich ärgern (to be annoyed) and sich aufregen (to get upset). They follow the pattern you know. Sich aufregen is separable, like aufstehen: the prefix goes to the end of the sentence. Ich rege mich auf.
cards.lead: The introduction promised a whole group of verbs. Start with three that you will need every day in the WG: for happy, annoyed and upset moments.

deeper.text: The verb forms are regular. Freuen and ärgern take the normal endings: freue, freust, freut. Aufregen is separable: the verb is second, the pronoun comes right after the verb, and the prefix auf stands at the very end. Look at it in a question too: Regst du dich auf? The prefix still goes to the end.

example.de: Du regst dich nicht auf.
example.en: You do not get upset.

cards.more: Put the little word in the box right behind the verb, always. For a separable verb, the prefix leaves and goes to the end of the sentence, so the sentence has a front part (rege mich) and an end part (auf). A common slip is Ich rege auf mich. The pronoun cannot wait behind the prefix. Say Ich rege mich auf, with mich directly after the verb.

cards.title: sich freuen auf or über?
cards.body: With sich freuen you often say what you are happy about. Auf is for something ahead of you, a plan, a party, the weekend. Über is for something already here or just past, a gift, a message, a visit. Both are followed by the accusative: Ich freue mich auf das Fest. Ben freut sich über das Geschenk.
cards.lead: You can say you are happy. Now you learn two small words that say what you are happy about, and how to choose between them.

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf das Fest.
examples.en: I am looking forward to the party.

examples.de: Ben freut sich über das Geschenk.
examples.en: Ben is happy about the present.

examples.de: Wir freuen uns auf den Urlaub.
examples.en: We are looking forward to the holiday.

deeper.text: The pair is easy to remember with time: auf looks forward, über looks at what is here. Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende, because it is not here yet. When a gift is on the table, you say Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. Learn auf and über as blocks with sich freuen. Both take the accusative.

example.de: Anna freut sich über die Nachricht.
example.en: Anna is happy about the message.

cards.more: Ask one question: is the thing here, or is it still coming? If it is still coming (the party next week), say auf. If it is here or already happened (the present on the table), say über. Then add the accusative article: das Fest, den Urlaub, die Nachricht. You do not need any other prepositions for sich freuen right now.
steps: Step 1: say Ich freue mich ...
Step 2: is it ahead? Say auf. Is it here or past? Say über.
Step 3: add the thing in the accusative: das Fest, das Geschenk.

cards.title: Calm and stress: sich beeilen, beruhigen, entspannen, erholen
cards.body: Four verbs for stress and rest: sich beeilen (to hurry), sich beruhigen (to calm down), sich entspannen (to relax) and sich erholen (to recover, to rest). They are all regular and follow the same pattern. Today you only use them in statements: Anna entspannt sich im Park.
cards.lead: Joy and anger are one side of the day. Now the other side: hurrying and calming down. These four verbs are the ones you use when the day is too long.

deeper.text: Sich entspannen and sich erholen are close, but not the same. Entspannen is to become loose, to let go, for example on the sofa or in the park. Erholen is to get your power back after a hard time, for example during holiday. You can often use both, but Ich erhole mich im Urlaub is the typical sentence.

example.de: Wir erholen uns im Urlaub.
example.en: We recover on holiday.

cards.more: Think about a phone with a battery. Sich beeilen is the fast-forward button. Sich beruhigen is the pause button. Sich entspannen is the screen-off mode, and sich erholen is charging the battery. All of them take the little word right after the verb: Ich beruhige mich. Mira beruhigt sich langsam. You only need to put the right little word behind the verb.

cards.title: Boring and surprising: sich langweilen, sich wundern
cards.body: Two more verbs for feelings in the middle of the day: sich langweilen (to be bored) and sich wundern (to be surprised, to wonder). Both follow the pattern: Leon langweilt sich. Ich wundere mich. With sich wundern you can add what surprised you: Anna wundert sich über das Wetter. Learn über as a block.
cards.lead: You can talk about joy, anger and rest. Two last verbs cover the quiet moments: when nothing happens, and when something is odd.

examples.de: Anna wundert sich über das Wetter.
examples.en: Anna is surprised about the weather.

deeper.text: Sich wundern does not mean that you are happy or sad, only that something is not what you expected. You can use it in a polite way too: Ich wundere mich über die Antwort. After über you say the accusative: das Wetter, die Antwort. This is the same block you learned for sich freuen über.

example.de: Ich wundere mich über die Antwort.
example.en: I am surprised about the answer.

cards.more: Langweilen is the quiet verb: nothing happens, the clock moves slowly, you check your phone. Wundern is the surprised verb: something is different from what you thought. Both take mich, dich, sich, uns, euch. If you want to say what surprised you, use über and the accusative, the same way as with freuen über. One block, two verbs.
steps: Step 1: say Ich wundere mich.
Step 2: what surprised you? Add über and the accusative.
Result: Ich wundere mich über das Wetter.

cards.title: Falling in love: sich verlieben in
cards.body: Sich verlieben means to fall in love. Add in plus the accusative to say with whom or what: Anna verliebt sich in die Stadt. Learn in plus the accusative as a block after sich verlieben, and use it with places and hobbies as well as people: Ben verliebt sich in die Musik.
cards.lead: You have joy, rest and surprise. Now one last feeling, a happy one: falling in love, with a person, a city or a hobby.

examples.de: Anna verliebt sich in die Stadt.
examples.en: Anna falls in love with the city.

examples.de: Ben verliebt sich in die Musik.
examples.en: Ben falls in love with the music.

examples.de: Du verliebst dich in den Park.
examples.en: You fall in love with the park.

deeper.text: In German you can fall in love with things and places too, not only with people, and it sounds natural: Ich verliebe mich in Berlin. The word in is always followed by the accusative here, because you move towards the new love. Like ordinary verbs, it is regular.

example.de: Wir verlieben uns in das Café.
example.en: We fall in love with the café.

cards.more: Sich verlieben is a verb with a direction. You are moving from not in love to in love, so German says in and the accusative, the direction case. You can remember it as a little jump into the thing: in die Stadt, in die Musik. English says with, but German says in. Learn the whole block as one piece.

rows: Anna verliebt sich in die Stadt.
Ich freue mich auf das Fest.

cards.title: Reflexive or not? Yourself or someone else
cards.body: Some verbs work both ways. Waschen: Ich wasche das Auto (another thing) or Ich wasche mich (myself). Ärgern: Ben ärgert Leon (Ben makes Leon angry) or Ben ärgert sich (Ben is annoyed). If someone or something else gets the action, use a noun or a name. If it is the same person, use the reflexive pronoun.
cards.lead: You know ten reflexive verbs. The last card shows the difference between doing something to yourself and doing it to someone else.

deeper.text: In the dictionary, sich in front marks verbs that mostly come with the reflexive pronoun, like sich freuen or sich beeilen. You cannot freuen another person in this pattern. Verbs like waschen and ärgern work both ways, so check the little word each time. If you see a name or a noun, it is another person or thing. If you see mich, dich or sich, it is the same person.

example.de: Mira wäscht sich.
example.en: Mira washes herself.

cards.more: Ask who gets the action. If you wash the car, the car gets it, so you say das Auto. If you wash yourself, you get it, so you say mich. The same with Ben: if Ben makes Leon angry, Leon gets the action and you say Leon. If Ben is angry himself, say sich. The new colour is your clue: if you see it, the person is doing the action to themselves.

lessons.title: Beeil dich! Reflexive verbs in Perfekt, with modals and as orders
lessons.goal: Use reflexive verbs in every sentence type (Perfekt, modals, orders) and sound happy, surprised or annoyed.

grammar.topic: reflexive verbs in every sentence type
grammar.point: Reflexive verbs build the Perfekt with haben: Ich habe mich gefreut. With a modal the pronoun comes after the subject and the infinitive goes to the end: Ich muss mich beeilen. An order starts with the verb and takes the pronoun right after it: Beeil dich! Beeilt euch! Setzen Sie sich!
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe mich beeilt. Beeil dich! Reflexive verbs always take haben.

mistake.why: Reflexive verbs always form the Perfekt with haben, never with sein: ich habe mich, du hast dich, er hat sich, then the participle at the end.

terms.meaning: the past tense for talking: haben or sein plus the participle at the end
the form for an order or a request: Beeil dich!
the melody of your voice, which shows how you feel

cards.title: Before we start: hurry up, Ben!
cards.body: It is 7:45, Ben is not dressed and the bus leaves at 8. Now you need reflexive verbs in every form: Ich beeile mich, Beeil dich! and Ich habe mich beeilt. Today you use them in the Perfekt, with modals and as orders, and you learn how to sound happy, surprised or annoyed.
steps: You already know: Ich beeile mich, and mich, dich, sich, uns, euch.
New today: Perfekt (Ich habe mich beeilt), modals (Ich muss mich beeilen), orders (Beeil dich!) and the melody of feelings.
By the end you can: use reflexive verbs in every sentence type and sound like you mean it.
cards.more: Imagine a little word that sticks to its verb like a magnet. Wherever the verb goes, the little word comes along: to the end in an order (Beeil dich!), after haben in the Perfekt (habe mich beeilt), after muss in a modal sentence (muss mich beeilen). You do not learn new little words, only where they sit. The next cards show each place, one at a time, then the melody of feelings in speech.

cards.title: Morning in the WG: getting ready
cards.body: In the morning you do many things to yourself: sich anziehen (get dressed), sich ausziehen (get undressed), sich kämmen, sich schminken, sich rasieren, sich setzen (sit down) and sich hinlegen (lie down). Two are separable: Ich ziehe mich an, Leon legt sich hin. The others are regular: Ben rasiert sich.
cards.lead: Hurrying is only one reason to use your reflexive verbs. Here are seven more for a normal morning in the WG, and then you can use them in the Perfekt.

deeper.text: You know sitzen from A1: Ich sitze am Tisch (I am sitting). Sich setzen means the moment you sit down: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl, dann sitze ich. In the same way sich hinlegen is the moment you lie down, and liegen is the state. German has two verbs for what English does with one: sit down and sit.

example.de: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
example.en: I sit down on the chair.

cards.more: Imagine a film of your morning. First you get up and sich anziehen: dressing. Then sich kämmen and sich rasieren or sich schminken, then you sich setzen at the table. In the evening you sich ausziehen and sich hinlegen. In each case you are the one who does it, and you are the one who gets it, so the little word is always mich, dich or sich. The separable ones send their prefix to the end.

cards.title: The Perfekt: always with haben
cards.body: Reflexive verbs build the Perfekt with haben, never with sein. Order: haben, then the reflexive pronoun, and the participle at the end. Ich habe mich gefreut. Ben hat sich angezogen. Wir haben uns beeilt. The participle works as for any other verb: gefreut, beeilt, and with a separable verb angezogen.
cards.lead: You can use reflexive verbs now. The same verbs must also tell what happened this morning, and for that you need the Perfekt.

deeper.text: It does not matter that English says I am dressed or I have sat down. In German the helper is always haben with these verbs: Ich habe mich gesetzt, Ich habe mich hingelegt. Sein is only for verbs of movement or change, and the reflexive verbs do not belong there. If you are not sure about a reflexive verb, use haben, because it is right every time.

example.de: Ich habe mich hingelegt.
example.en: I lay down.

cards.more: The Perfekt is a sandwich: the helper verb haben is the first slice, the participle is the last slice, and the little word goes right behind the helper. In a reflexive Perfekt the helper is always haben. The only job is to place mich, dich, sich, uns or euch right behind it: ich habe mich, du hast dich, er hat sich. A wrong sentence is Ich bin mich beeilt. Say Ich habe mich beeilt.

cards.title: With modals: muss, soll, will, kann
cards.body: In a sentence with a modal the modal is in second place and the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive. The reflexive pronoun comes right after the subject: Ich muss mich beeilen. Du sollst dich setzen. Wir wollen uns entspannen. In a question the order is Kannst du dich konzentrieren?
cards.lead: You know the Perfekt. The last sentence type is the modal sentence, for what you must, should or want to do to yourself.

deeper.text: When a name follows the verb in the sentence, the little word comes before the name, as you learned in lesson 1: Heute muss sich Ben beeilen. The infinitive still stays at the end. This is the same order as in Heute fühlt sich Mira besser. A modal sentence also works as a question: Müssen wir uns beeilen? The infinitive is always the last word.

example.de: Heute muss sich Ben beeilen.
example.en: Today Ben must hurry.

cards.more: In a modal sentence there are two verbs, and they sit like two bookends: the modal is in position 2, the infinitive is at the end. The little word is not a bookend, it sits right after the subject, next to the modal. Say it out loud: ich muss mich beeilen, du sollst dich setzen, wir wollen uns entspannen. The pronoun never goes behind the infinitive.
steps: Step 1: subject, then the modal in second place.
Step 2: the reflexive pronoun right behind them.
Step 3: the main verb as an infinitive at the end.

cards.title: Orders: Beeil dich! Beeilt euch! Setzen Sie sich!
cards.body: An order uses the verb first and the reflexive pronoun right after it. To a friend (du): Beeil dich! To friends (ihr): Beeilt euch! Polite (Sie): Setzen Sie sich bitte! Beruhig dich! means Calm down! A separable verb sends its prefix to the end: Zieh dich an!
cards.lead: You use the little word in statements, in the Perfekt and with modals. Now the quickest sentence of all: the order, for Ben and for guests.

deeper.text: With du, the order is the stem of the verb: beeilen becomes Beeil, setzen becomes Setz. A little e at the end is possible but sounds stiff. With ihr you keep -t: Beeilt euch. With Sie you say the verb and Sie and the pronoun: Beeilen Sie sich! Separable verbs behave as in A1: Zieh dich an!, Zieht euch an!

example.de: Zieh dich an!
example.en: Get dressed!

cards.more: Think of the order as a short cut: you cut the subject. Instead of Du beeilst dich you say Beeil dich. The verb comes first, the little word right after. The little word stays: for du it is dich, for ihr it is euch, for Sie it is sich. A common slip is Beeil! alone. This is incomplete, because the verb needs its partner. Say Beeil dich!

cards.title: Polite and social: bedanken, verabschieden, konzentrieren
cards.body: Three verbs for polite moments: sich bedanken (to say thank you), sich verabschieden (to say goodbye) and sich konzentrieren (to concentrate). To say what you thank for, use für and the accusative. To say whom you thank, use bei: Ich bedanke mich bei Frau Weber. Learn both as blocks.
cards.lead: You can order, report and plan with reflexive verbs. The last verbs you need are the ones for polite moments, when somebody gives you something or you leave.

examples.de: Ich bedanke mich für das Geschenk.
examples.en: I say thank you for the present.

deeper.text: You can use both blocks in one sentence: Ich bedanke mich bei Frau Weber für die Torte. Bei names the person, für names the thing. The person has no article change here, because names do not take one. You will use this in the next lessons, whenever someone gives you a gift or helps you.

example.de: Ich bedanke mich bei Frau Weber für die Torte.
example.en: I thank Frau Weber for the cake.

cards.more: To thank someone you do two things: you say who you thank and what for. German has a short word for each: bei for the person, für for the thing. If you leave one out, the sentence still works: Ich bedanke mich. The other two verbs are easy: Wir verabschieden uns when we leave, and Mira konzentriert sich when she learns. You only need the little word right behind the verb.

rows: Ich bedanke mich für das Geschenk.

cards.title: Pronunciation: sound happy, surprised or annoyed
cards.body: The same word can sound happy or bored, and the melody tells the listener how you feel. Find the feeling word, stress it, and choose the melody. Happy: high and loud. Surprised: the voice goes up at the end. Annoyed: a hard stress on the feeling word. Sad: low and slow.
cards.lead: You have the verbs and the little word. The last card is about sound: how your voice tells the listener whether you are glad or annoyed.

examples.en: That annoys me! (annoyed: stress on ärgert)
examples.why: Here mich is a plain object, not reflexive: das is the subject.

deeper.text: The same word can say the opposite: Super! with a high, loud voice is happy, but Na super. with a flat, low voice means Oh great, said with annoyance. On paper the punctuation helps: an exclamation mark means strong feeling, a question mark with a raised voice means surprise, a full stop means calm or flat.

example.de: Na super.
example.en: Oh great. (annoyed, flat voice)

cards.more: Imagine a volume dial and a pitch dial. For joy you turn both up. For surprise you turn the pitch up at the end of the word. For annoyance you push the volume on the feeling word, but keep the pitch low. For sadness you turn both down and slow down. Practice with one word: say Super! four times, with four feelings, and listen to the difference.
steps: Step 1: find the feeling word in the sentence.
Step 2: stress it: say it louder and longer.
Step 3: choose the melody: up for joy and surprise, down and slow for sadness.

lessons.title: Wenn ich traurig bin …: conditions with wenn
lessons.goal: Say what you do in a situation or under a condition with wenn, with the verb at the end, and start a sentence with a wenn clause.

grammar.point: Wenn (if) opens a condition. In the wenn clause the conjugated verb goes to the end; a modal goes after the infinitive, a separable verb is one word, haben/sein goes after the participle. If the wenn clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
grammar.oneLine: Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett. Verb at the end, then verb first.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ich bin müde, ich gehe ins Bett.
mistake.right: Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
mistake.why: In the wenn clause the verb goes to the end (müde bin). The wenn clause is position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb (gehe ich).

terms.meaning: the situation in which something happens: wenn es regnet
the part of the sentence after wenn, with the conjugated verb at the end
the part that can stand alone: ich bleibe zu Hause

cards.title: Before we start: if this, then that
cards.body: You can already give a reason with weil and say what you think with dass. Both push the verb to the end. Today you meet a third word that works the same way: wenn (if). With it you say what you do in a situation: Ich bleibe zu Hause, wenn ich müde bin.
steps: You already know: weil and dass, with the verb at the end (…, weil ich müde bin).
New today: wenn (if) for a condition, and a sentence that starts with wenn.
By the end you can: say what you do when you are sad, tired, lucky or unlucky.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: You know this already: weil gives a reason.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Mira traurig ist.
examples.en: I think that Mira is sad.
examples.why: You know this already: dass, verb at the end.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, wenn ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home if I am tired.
examples.why: New today: wenn, same order as weil.

cards.more: Weil says why something is true now: I am tired, so I stay at home. Wenn says what happens in a situation: if I am tired, I stay at home, and if I am not, I go out. The word order is your old friend: comma, wenn, subject, the rest, verb at the end. The new step today is a sentence that begins with wenn.

cards.title: Wenn means if: the verb goes to the end
cards.body: Wenn opens a condition: the main clause happens only if the wenn part is true. The word order is the same as with weil and dass: main clause, comma, wenn, subject, the rest, then the conjugated verb at the very end. The verb end has its own colour.
cards.lead: The introduction put weil and wenn side by side. This card shows wenn on its own, so that you see the condition and the verb at the end clearly.

examples.de: Ich gehe spazieren, wenn das Wetter schön ist.
examples.en: I go for a walk if the weather is nice.

examples.de: Mira ruft dich an, wenn sie Zeit hat.
examples.en: Mira calls you if she has time.

examples.de: Wir kochen zusammen, wenn Leon Hunger hat.
examples.en: We cook together if Leon is hungry.

deeper.text: In English, if and when are two words, and German wann is a question word: Wann kommst du? Wenn is never a question. It joins two parts of one sentence, and the part after wenn is a condition or a situation. If you can ask in English “and only then?”, wenn is the right word.

example.de: Wann kommst du? Ich komme, wenn ich Zeit habe.
example.en: When are you coming? I am coming when I have time.

cards.more: Think of a door with a sign: the main clause only walks through if the wenn part says yes. Ich gehe spazieren is the plan. Wenn das Wetter schön ist is the sign on the door. Inside the wenn part, the verb waits at the very end, just like after weil and dass, which you already know well.
steps: Step 1: the main clause: Ich gehe spazieren.
Step 2: a comma, then wenn.
Step 3: the subject and the rest: das Wetter schön.
Step 4: the conjugated verb at the very end: ist.

cards.title: Wenn with a modal, a separable verb and the Perfekt
cards.body: With a modal, the infinitive stands before it and the modal goes to the very end: wenn ich lernen muss. A separable verb is one word again at the end: wenn Leon anruft. In the Perfekt, the participle comes first and haben or sein goes last: wenn du gegessen hast.
cards.lead: You can put a simple verb at the end of a wenn clause. Now the verb has two parts, so you learn which part goes last and which waits just before it.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, wenn ich lernen muss.
examples.en: I stay at home if I have to study.

examples.de: Mira ist froh, wenn Leon anruft.
examples.en: Mira is happy if Leon calls.

examples.de: Wir gehen los, wenn du gegessen hast.
examples.en: We leave when you have eaten.

deeper.text: The rule is the same in all three cases: the conjugated verb, the one that changes with the person, is the very last word. Everything else stays in front of it. That is why you say wenn du kommen kannst and wenn er aufgestanden ist. The separable prefix joins its verb again, because nothing stands between them.

example.de: Ich helfe dir, wenn du mich brauchst.
example.en: I help you if you need me.

cards.more: A common slip is wenn ich muss lernen, because in a normal sentence muss comes second. In a wenn clause it walks to the very end: wenn ich lernen muss. Ask: which verb changes with the person? Muss, kann, hat, ist. That one goes last. The other verb, lernen or gegessen, waits right in front of it. A separable verb like anrufen simply becomes one word again: wenn Leon anruft.

cards.title: Wenn first: then the main clause starts with its verb
cards.body: You can start with the wenn clause. Then the whole wenn clause is position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb: Wenn ich traurig bin, rufe ich Mira an. In the middle two verbs stand side by side, with a comma between them: bin, rufe.
cards.lead: Your wenn clause so far always came second. Now you move it to the front, which Germans do very often, and the main clause changes its order.

examples.de: Wenn ich traurig bin, rufe ich Mira an.
examples.en: If I am sad, I call Mira.

examples.de: Wenn Ben müde ist, geht er ins Bett.
examples.en: If Ben is tired, he goes to bed.

examples.de: Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.en: If it rains, we stay at home.

deeper.text: This is the old verb-second rule from A1. In Heute gehe ich ins Kino, heute is position 1 and the verb comes second. A wenn clause is just a long position 1. So the main clause starts with the verb, and the subject follows it. Verb, comma, verb: that pattern in the middle tells you the sentence is right.

example.de: Heute gehe ich ins Kino.
example.en: Today I am going to the cinema.

cards.more: Picture the wenn clause as one big box at the front of the sentence. A box at the front uses up position 1, just like heute or am Montag. So what comes next? The verb, always. Say it aloud: wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich. Bin, gehe: two verbs, one comma. If the subject comes right after the comma (wenn ich müde bin, ich gehe), the sentence is wrong.
steps: Step 1: the wenn clause, verb at the end: Wenn ich traurig bin,
Step 2: the main clause starts with its verb: rufe
Step 3: then the subject and the rest: ich Mira an.

cards.title: Feelings with wenn: when I cry, when you smile
cards.body: Wenn is perfect for feelings, because feelings come in situations: Ich bin glücklich, wenn … Two new verbs fit here: weinen (to cry) and lächeln (to smile). A tear is die Träne. Use them in both orders: Ich weine, wenn ich traurig bin. Wenn Ben lächelt, ist die Stimmung gut.
cards.lead: You can build a wenn clause in both orders now. Next you use it for what this chapter is about: feelings, and two verbs that show them.

examples.de: Ich bin glücklich, wenn meine Freunde da sind.
examples.en: I am happy when my friends are there.

examples.de: Anna weint, wenn sie traurig ist.
examples.en: Anna cries when she is sad.

examples.de: Wenn Ben lächelt, ist die Stimmung gut.
examples.en: When Ben smiles, the mood is good.

deeper.text: Weinen and lächeln are regular: ich weine, du weinst, er weint; ich lächle, du lächelst, er lächelt. Lächeln drops the e in the ich form, like sammeln: ich sammle. In the Perfekt both take haben: Ich habe geweint, Sie hat gelächelt. Lachen is a big laugh, lächeln is a small smile.

example.de: Mira hat gelächelt, aber Leon hat gelacht.
example.en: Mira smiled, but Leon laughed.

cards.more: Think of a little film for each feeling. Sad: tears, die Tränen, and you cry, du weinst. Happy: a small smile, du lächelst, or a big laugh, du lachst. Wenn gives the film its scene: wenn Anna traurig ist, weint sie. You choose the scene, the feeling verb follows.

cards.title: A reflexive verb inside the wenn clause
cards.body: Reflexive verbs work in a wenn clause too. The pronoun comes right after the subject, and the verb still goes last: …, wenn ich mich ärgere. With a name it is the same: wenn Anna sich freut. Only the order of the verb changes, the little pronoun stays next to the subject.
cards.lead: You know the reflexive verbs from lessons 1 to 3. Now you put them inside a wenn clause, where the pronoun sits right behind the subject.

examples.de: Ich gehe spazieren, wenn ich mich ärgere.
examples.en: I go for a walk when I am annoyed.

examples.de: Wenn Anna sich freut, singt sie.
examples.en: When Anna is happy, she sings.

examples.de: Wenn du dich beeilst, kommst du pünktlich.
examples.en: If you hurry, you will be on time.

deeper.text: A separable reflexive verb follows both rules: the pronoun after the subject, the verb as one word at the end. So: wenn ich mich aufrege. With a modal the infinitive comes before the modal: wenn du dich beeilen musst. In the main clause after the comma the pronoun comes right after the subject: Wenn es regnet, ärgere ich mich.

example.de: Wenn es regnet, ärgert Ben sich.
example.en: If it rains, Ben gets annoyed.

cards.more: Keep the pronoun as close to the subject as a shadow: ich mich, du dich, Anna sich. In the wenn clause that pair comes first, then the rest, then the verb last: wenn ich mich freue. If you are unsure, say the short sentence first, Ich freue mich, and then send freue to the end: wenn ich mich freue.
steps: Step 1: wenn, then the subject: wenn Anna
Step 2: the reflexive pronoun right after it: sich
Step 3: the rest of the clause, then the verb last: freut.

cards.title: Good luck, bad luck: Glück, Pech and Erfolg
cards.body: Three useful blocks: Glück haben (to be lucky), Pech haben (to be unlucky), Erfolg haben (to be successful). Ärger means trouble. Gut gelaunt or schlecht gelaunt says someone’s mood. Friends help: trösten (to comfort), umarmen (to hug). Wishes: Viel Glück! Viel Erfolg!
cards.lead: You can talk about feelings in a wenn clause. Last, you get the words for lucky and unlucky days and for helping a sad friend, so your wenn sentences can say more.

examples.de: Wenn ich Pech habe, tröstet mich Mira.
examples.en: If I am unlucky, Mira comforts me.

examples.de: Ben ist gut gelaunt, wenn er Erfolg hat.
examples.en: Ben is in a good mood when he is successful.

examples.de: Wenn Leon traurig ist, umarmt Anna ihn.
examples.en: When Leon is sad, Anna hugs him.

deeper.text: Glück has two meanings: luck (Ich habe Glück) and happiness (Das ist Glück!). Pech is only bad luck, and both have no plural. Ärger means trouble with someone: Ich habe Ärger mit Ben. It is not the same as sich ärgern, but the two belong together: wenn ich Ärger habe, ärgere ich mich.

example.de: Ich habe Ärger mit Ben.
example.en: I have trouble with Ben.

cards.more: Imagine a coin. One side says Glück: the bus comes right away, you win a game, Glück gehabt! The other side says Pech: the bus has left, it rains. Erfolg is what you earn by working hard. When a friend has Pech, you help: you comfort them, trösten, and maybe hug them, umarmen. And before a test you say Viel Glück! or Viel Erfolg!

lessons.title: Immer wenn …: repeated events, a quarrel and making up
lessons.goal: Say what always happens with (immer) wenn and wenn … dann, describe a quarrel, say sorry and make up.

grammar.topic: wenn for repeated events; reflexive quarrel verbs
grammar.point: Wenn also means whenever. Immer wenn makes this clear. The word order stays the same: verb at the end of the wenn clause, verb first in the main clause. After the comma you can add dann, then the verb: Wenn Mira schlechte Laune hat, dann ist sie still. Sich streiten, sich entschuldigen, sich vertragen and sich schämen are reflexive.
grammar.oneLine: Immer wenn Leon kocht, ist die Küche schmutzig. Wir streiten uns.

mistake.why: When people argue with each other, streiten is reflexive: wir streiten uns, sie streiten sich. The pronoun shows that both sides are in the quarrel.

terms.meaning: something that happens again and again: immer wenn es regnet
a verb with mich, dich, sich, uns or euch: sich streiten
saying sorry: Entschuldige bitte!

cards.title: Before we start: every time Leon cooks …
cards.body: In lesson 4 wenn meant if: Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett. Wenn has a second job. It also means whenever, every time: something happens again and again. In a WG that is useful, because the same things happen every week, and sometimes the same quarrels. Today the WG argues, says sorry and makes up.
steps: You already know: wenn = if, verb at the end, and a main clause that starts with its verb.
New today: wenn = every time, immer wenn, wenn … dann, and verbs for a quarrel and making up.
By the end you can: say what always happens, argue a little, say sorry and make up.

examples.de: Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
examples.en: If I am tired, I go to bed.
examples.why: You know this already: wenn = if.
You know this already: a reflexive verb.

examples.de: Immer wenn Leon kocht, ist die Küche schmutzig.
examples.en: Every time Leon cooks, the kitchen is dirty.

cards.more: English uses two words: if (maybe it happens) and whenever (it happens again and again). German uses wenn for both, and the word order does not change at all. Put immer in front, immer wenn, and everybody hears: this happens every time. Then you get the words for a small WG quarrel and for saying sorry.

cards.title: Immer wenn: every time something happens
cards.body: Wenn can also mean whenever: an event that happens again and again. To make that clear, put immer in front: immer wenn. The word order is exactly the same as in lesson 4: verb at the end of the wenn clause, and if it comes first, the main clause starts with its verb.
cards.lead: The introduction showed that wenn has a second meaning. This card shows how immer wenn marks a repeated event, with the word order you already know.

examples.de: Immer wenn Ben Musik hört, singt er.
examples.en: Every time Ben listens to music, he sings.

examples.de: Immer wenn es regnet, ist Anna schlecht gelaunt.
examples.en: Every time it rains, Anna is in a bad mood.

deeper.text: Without immer, the context tells you which meaning wenn has. Mira lacht, wenn Leon tanzt can mean if or whenever, and both are fine, because Leon dances often. Immer before wenn removes all doubt. It stands before the conjunction and counts together with the wenn clause as position 1.

example.de: Immer wenn wir feiern, tanzt Leon.
example.en: Every time we celebrate, Leon dances.

cards.more: Think of a habit, something on repeat like a song. Every time Ben hears music, he sings. That is immer wenn. In lesson 4 you had a door with a sign: if yes, go through. Now the door opens every day at the same time. Same door, same order of words, but it happens again and again.
steps: Step 1: immer wenn, then the subject: Immer wenn Ben
Step 2: the rest, verb last: Musik hört,
Step 3: the main clause starts with its verb: singt er.

cards.title: Wenn … dann: dann after the comma
cards.body: After a wenn clause you can add dann (then) at the start of the main clause. Dann is position 1 of the main clause, so the verb follows it right away, and then the subject: Wenn Mira schlechte Laune hat, dann ist sie still. Dann makes the link stronger, but you can always leave it out.
cards.lead: You know immer wenn for repeated events. Now you add dann after the comma, a small word Germans like, and you see where the verb goes after it.

examples.de: Wenn Mira schlechte Laune hat, dann ist sie still.
examples.en: When Mira is in a bad mood, then she is quiet.

examples.de: Wenn Ben Hunger hat, dann kocht er.
examples.en: When Ben is hungry, then he cooks.

examples.de: Wenn du Zeit hast, dann gehen wir ins Kino.
examples.en: If you have time, then we go to the cinema.

deeper.text: You know dann from A1 stories: Zuerst frühstücke ich, dann gehe ich los. It works the same after a wenn clause: dann takes the first place, the verb the second. Dann works with both meanings of wenn, if and whenever. Without dann the main clause starts with the verb: Wenn Ben Hunger hat, kocht er.

example.de: Zuerst frühstücke ich, dann gehe ich los.
example.en: First I have breakfast, then I leave.

cards.more: Dann is like a small arrow: if this, then that. After the arrow, German wants the verb, not the subject. A common slip is Wenn Mira schlechte Laune hat, dann sie ist still. Say it like a story with dann from A1: dann ist sie still. Dann, verb, subject. If you are not sure, just leave dann out: Wenn …, ist sie still.

rows: Wenn Ben Hunger hat, kocht er.
Wenn Ben Hunger hat, dann kocht er.
Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir hier.
Wenn es regnet, dann bleiben wir hier.

cards.title: A WG quarrel: sich streiten
cards.body: A quarrel is der Streit. The verb is reflexive: sich streiten (to argue). Leon und Ben streiten sich. Somebody who is annoyed is sauer (colloquial). Somebody whose feelings are hurt is beleidigt. Often it all starts with a misunderstanding: das Missverständnis.
cards.lead: You can say what happens every time. Now the WG has a quarrel, so you learn the words to describe it, starting with a reflexive verb you will use a lot.

deeper.text: Sich streiten has a strong Perfekt: Wir haben uns gestritten. Like all reflexive verbs, it takes haben. With whom? Mit plus dative: Ich streite mich mit Ben. Without sich the verb sounds wrong when you mean with each other. So learn the whole block: sich streiten, hat sich gestritten.

example.de: Gestern haben wir uns gestritten.
example.en: Yesterday we argued.

cards.more: Picture two people pulling one rope. Each pulls, and the rope pulls back: that is why German says streiten sich, they argue with each other. The little word uns or sich shows that both sides are in it. Sauer is the face of the person who is angry, beleidigt is the face of the person who feels hurt.

cards.title: Saying sorry: Das ist meine Schuld
cards.body: To say sorry you use sich entschuldigen: Ich entschuldige mich. To someone: bei plus dative: Ich entschuldige mich bei dir. Short and spoken: Entschuldige bitte! If it was you: Das ist meine Schuld. The other person can answer with verzeihen (to forgive): Ich verzeihe dir.
cards.lead: The quarrel happened. Now somebody has to say sorry, so you learn the reflexive verb for apologising and two short blocks that make peace.

deeper.text: Verzeihen takes the dative, like helfen and danken: Ich verzeihe dir, Mira verzeiht ihm. Its Perfekt is irregular: Ich habe dir verziehen. You know die Entschuldigung from A1: Entschuldigung! is a short polite sorry to anyone, Entschuldige bitte! is warmer and for a friend you say du to.

example.de: Ben hat Leon verziehen.
example.en: Ben forgave Leon.

cards.more: An apology has two halves, like a handshake. One person says: Entschuldige bitte, das ist meine Schuld. The other person takes the hand: Ich verzeihe dir. Bei dir means to you, the person who gets the sorry. Learn the pieces as blocks and say them aloud: they sound kind and they work.

rows: Entschuldige bitte! Das ist meine Schuld.

cards.title: Making up: Alles wieder gut!
cards.body: After a quarrel you make up: sich vertragen. Wir vertragen uns wieder. Sometimes you feel bad about what you said: sich schämen, Ich schäme mich. And at the end everyone is happy: Alles wieder gut! The WG story has three scenes: schlechte Laune, die Nachricht, alles wieder gut.
cards.lead: Someone said sorry. Now the friends make up, and you see the whole WG story in three short scenes from start to finish.

deeper.text: Sich vertragen changes its vowel like fahren: ich vertrage mich, du verträgst dich, er verträgt sich. The Perfekt is hat sich vertragen. It can also mean to get along: Ben und Leon vertragen sich gut. Sich schämen is regular: ich schäme mich, Perfekt hat sich geschämt.

example.de: Ben und Leon vertragen sich gut.
example.en: Ben and Leon get along well.

cards.more: Here is the little WG film. Scene 1, Schlechte Laune: the kitchen is dirty again, Ben is sauer, Leon is beleidigt. Scene 2, Die Nachricht: Leon writes, Entschuldige bitte, das ist meine Schuld, ich schäme mich. Scene 3, Alles wieder gut: they meet in the kitchen, cook together and say, Wir vertragen uns wieder.
steps: Scene 1, Schlechte Laune: Ben und Leon streiten sich.
Scene 2, Die Nachricht: Entschuldige bitte! Das ist meine Schuld.
Scene 3, Alles wieder gut: Wir vertragen uns wieder.

cards.title: Put it together: wenn, reflexive and Perfekt
cards.body: Now combine the parts of this chapter. A reflexive verb in the wenn clause: Wenn wir uns streiten, … The pronoun stands after the subject, the verb at the end. The main clause starts with its verb, and it can be in the Perfekt: Wenn wir uns gestritten haben, sind wir immer traurig.
cards.lead: You have every piece now: wenn in two meanings, dann, and reflexive verbs for quarrels. This last card puts them together in longer sentences.

examples.de: Wenn wir uns streiten, sind wir danach immer traurig.
examples.en: Whenever we argue, we are always sad afterwards.

examples.de: Wenn Leon sich entschuldigt, verzeiht Ben ihm.
examples.en: When Leon apologises, Ben forgives him.

examples.de: Immer wenn wir uns gestritten haben, vertragen wir uns schnell.
examples.en: Every time we have argued, we make up quickly.

deeper.text: In the main clause after the comma the reflexive pronoun comes right after the subject: vertragen wir uns, verzeiht Ben ihm. In the wenn clause it comes right after the subject too: wenn wir uns streiten. In both halves the pronoun sticks to its subject. Only the verbs move: last in the wenn clause, first in the main clause.

example.de: Wenn ich mich schäme, entschuldige ich mich.
example.en: When I am ashamed, I apologise.

cards.more: Build it in three moves. First the short sentence: Wir streiten uns. Then the wenn version, with the verb at the end: wenn wir uns streiten. Then the main clause, verb first: sind wir traurig. Put a comma in the middle, and you have Wenn wir uns streiten, sind wir traurig. Check the middle: two verbs, one comma.
steps: Step 1: the short sentence: Wir streiten uns.
Step 2: the wenn clause, verb last: Wenn wir uns streiten,
Step 3: the main clause, verb first: sind wir danach traurig.

lessons.title: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! Congratulations, condolences and thanks
lessons.goal: Congratulate, show sympathy, thank, say what makes you glad or sorry, and write a short card.

grammar.topic: fixed phrases for occasions; zum/zur; Schade, dass …
grammar.point: Wishes for an occasion take zu plus dative: zum Geburtstag, zum Jubiläum, zur Hochzeit. Many phrases are fixed blocks: Herzlichen Glückwunsch!, Alles Gute!, Mein herzliches Beileid. Joy and regret often use dass with the verb at the end: Schade, dass du nicht kommen kannst.
grammar.oneLine: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zur Hochzeit! Schade, dass du nicht kommen kannst.

mistake.why: The occasion takes zu plus dative, not für: zur Hochzeit (die), zum Geburtstag (der), zum Jubiläum (das).

terms.meaning: a special moment such as a wedding or a farewell: der Anlass
a block of words you use as it is: Alles Gute!
words of sympathy after a death: Mein herzliches Beileid

cards.title: Before we start: the right words at the right moment
cards.body: Since A1 you can say Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! and Danke! Life has more moments than birthdays: a wedding, a farewell, an anniversary, and sometimes sad news. Today you learn short, fixed phrases for each one. They are the words Germans really say and write on a card, so learn them as blocks.
steps: You already know: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!, Danke!, gratulieren and dass with the verb at the end.
New today: phrases to congratulate, to show sympathy, to thank and to say what you regret.
By the end you can: write a short card for a wedding, an anniversary or a farewell.

examples.de: Ich freue mich sehr für dich.
examples.en: I am very happy for you.

examples.why: New today: a fixed phrase for sad news.

cards.more: Think of these phrases as keys. Each moment in life has its own key: a wedding has one, sad news has another. You do not build them word by word, you take the right key and use it. The cards go through the moments first, then congratulations, sympathy, thanks, joy and regret, and at the end a whole card text.

cards.title: Occasions: Hochzeit, Jubiläum, Abschied
cards.body: An occasion is der Anlass. Three new ones: die Hochzeit (wedding), das Jubiläum (anniversary of a firm or club), der Abschied (farewell). The verb heiraten means to marry. For the wish you use zu plus dative: zum Geburtstag, zum Jubiläum, zum Abschied, zur Hochzeit.
cards.lead: The introduction gave you the idea of the right words for each moment. First you need the names of the moments themselves, and the little word zum or zur.

examples.de: Mira und Leon gehen zur Hochzeit.
examples.en: Mira and Leon are going to the wedding.
Anna and Ben are getting married.

deeper.text: Zum is zu plus dem, for der and das words: zum Geburtstag, zum Jubiläum, zum Abschied. Zur is zu plus der, for die words: zur Hochzeit. This is the dative you know from zum Bahnhof and zur Arbeit. Das Jubiläum has an unusual plural: die Jubiläen.

example.de: Herr Ali feiert das Jubiläum im Restaurant.
example.en: Herr Ali celebrates the anniversary in the restaurant.

cards.more: Make a little calendar of life. A birthday every year: zum Geburtstag. A wedding, when two people marry: zur Hochzeit. An anniversary, when a shop is ten or twenty years old: zum Jubiläum. A farewell, when someone leaves: zum Abschied. The one thing that changes is zum or zur, and it follows der, die, das.

cards.title: Congratulating: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! Alles Gute!
cards.body: To congratulate: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zur Hochzeit! or Ich gratuliere dir (zu plus dative). To wish well: Alles Gute! Viel Glück! To share the joy: Ich freue mich für euch. These are fixed blocks, so do not change the endings: Herzlichen Glückwunsch is always the same.
cards.lead: You know the occasions. Next you learn the blocks to congratulate and wish well, so that you can say something warm at every occasion.

examples.en: I congratulate you on your anniversary.

deeper.text: Sich freuen has three partners now. Auf: something ahead, Ich freue mich auf die Party. Über: something that is here, Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. Für: another person’s good news, Ich freue mich für dich. Gratulieren takes the dative, like danken: Ich gratuliere Mira, ich gratuliere ihr.

example.de: Ich freue mich für Mira.
example.en: I am happy for Mira.

cards.more: Picture your friend with great news, a wedding or a new job. You say three things: first the key phrase, Herzlichen Glückwunsch!, then a wish, Alles Gute!, then your own feeling, Ich freue mich für dich. Three short blocks, and it sounds natural. Never write für after Glückwunsch: it is zum or zur.

cards.title: Sad news: Mein herzliches Beileid
cards.body: When someone has died, people say: Mein herzliches Beileid (my deepest sympathy) or simply Es tut mir sehr leid. Sterben means to die, Perfekt ist gestorben. Die Trauer is grief. Keep it short and polite; for Frau Weber, say Sie: Es tut mir sehr leid, Frau Weber.
cards.lead: Not every moment is happy. This card gives you the few short words for sad news, so that you can be kind and polite when it matters.

examples.de: Es tut mir sehr leid, Frau Weber.
examples.en: I am very sorry, Frau Weber.

deeper.text: Sterben changes its vowel: ich sterbe, du stirbst, er stirbt. Like gehen and fahren it takes sein in the Perfekt: ist gestorben. Beileid is for the death of a person and is a little formal. For a pet, Es tut mir so leid is warmer. Beileid and Trauer have no plural.

example.de: Die Trauer ist groß.
example.en: The grief is great.

cards.more: Here less is more. A few calm words are kinder than many. Say Es tut mir sehr leid, or write Mein herzliches Beileid on a card. Then offer help: Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an. That one sentence shows you care, and it uses the wenn you know from this chapter.
steps: Step 1: the feeling: Es tut mir sehr leid.
Step 2: on a card or for a person: Mein herzliches Beileid.
Step 3: offer help: Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an.

cards.title: Saying thank you: dankbar and sich bedanken
cards.body: You know Danke and Vielen Dank. For more: Vielen Dank für die Einladung! Ich bin dir sehr dankbar (grateful). Formal and written: Ich bedanke mich für … The answer to thanks: Gern geschehen! (you are welcome) or Kein Problem!
cards.lead: You can congratulate and show sympathy. Now someone helps you or invites you, so you learn several ways to thank them and to answer thanks.

examples.en: Thank you very much for the invitation!
I am very grateful to you.

deeper.text: Für plus accusative tells what you thank someone for: Danke für das Geschenk, Ich bedanke mich für die Hilfe. Dankbar takes the dative of the person: Ich bin dir dankbar, Ich bin Ihnen dankbar. Sich bedanken is a little more formal than danken, and you see it often in letters and speeches.

example.de: Ich bedanke mich für die Hilfe.
example.en: Thank you for the help.

cards.more: Thanks are a little ladder. The lowest step is Danke! Then Vielen Dank! Then Vielen Dank für die Hilfe! At the top, for something big: Ich bin dir sehr dankbar. When someone thanks you, catch it with a short answer: Gern geschehen! It is like saying: it was a pleasure.

cards.title: Joy and regret: Wie schön! Schade, dass …
cards.body: Joy: Wie schön! or Toll, dass du kommst! Regret: Schade, dass du nicht kommen kannst. Es tut mir leid, dass … The new verb bedauern means to regret and sounds polite: Ich bedauere, dass ich nicht kommen kann. After dass the verb goes to the end, as you know.
cards.lead: You know the dass clause from chapter 3. Here it helps you say what makes you glad or sorry, for example when you cannot come to a party.

examples.de: Schade, dass Leon nicht kommen kann.
examples.en: What a pity that Leon cannot come.

examples.de: Ich bedauere, dass ich keine Zeit habe.
examples.en: I regret that I have no time.

deeper.text: Schade, dass and Toll, dass are short forms of Es ist schade, dass and Es ist toll, dass. Both are very common in speech and on cards. Bedauern is regular: ich bedauere, hat bedauert. It is more formal than Es tut mir leid, so it fits a letter to Herr Ali or Frau Weber better than a message to Ben.

example.de: Es tut mir leid, dass ich so spät komme.
example.en: I am sorry that I am so late.

cards.more: Picture two faces. The happy face says Wie schön! or Toll, dass du da bist! The sorry face says Schade, dass … or Es tut mir leid, dass … A common slip is Schade, dass du kannst nicht kommen. Remember dass: the modal goes last, and the infinitive waits before it: dass du nicht kommen kannst.

rows: Schade, dass du nicht kommen kannst.
Ich bedauere, dass ich keine Zeit habe.

cards.title: A short card: greeting, wish, wenn and closing
cards.body: A card has four parts. 1. Greeting: Lieber Herr Ali, … 2. The wish: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Jubiläum! 3. A personal sentence, maybe with wenn: Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an! 4. Closing: Alles Gute! Viele Grüße, Mira. Short and warm is perfect.
cards.lead: You have every block now: occasions, wishes, sympathy, thanks, joy and regret. This last card puts them into one short card text, the way people really write it.

examples.de: Wenn du Hilfe brauchst, ruf mich an!
examples.en: If you need help, call me!

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf die Party.
examples.en: I am looking forward to the party.

deeper.text: After a wenn clause, an imperative also starts the main clause: Wenn du Hilfe brauchst, ruf mich an! With Sie: Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an! Lieber goes with a man, liebe with a woman: Lieber Herr Ali, liebe Frau Weber. The first word after the comma is small.

example.de: Liebe Frau Weber, es tut mir sehr leid.
example.en: Dear Frau Weber, I am very sorry.

cards.more: Write it like building a small house. The door is the greeting, Lieber Herr Ali. The main room is the wish, Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Jubiläum! A small window is one personal sentence, Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an. The roof is the closing: Alles Gute! Viele Grüße, Mira. Four parts, and your card is ready.
steps: Step 1: greeting: Lieber Herr Ali,
Step 2: the wish: herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Jubiläum!
Step 3: a personal sentence: Wenn Sie Hilfe brauchen, rufen Sie mich an!
Step 4: closing: Alles Gute! Viele Grüße, Mira

lessons.title: Frohe Weihnachten! Festivals through the year
lessons.goal: Name the big festivals and their wishes, say when they are and what people do, use wenn for yearly routines, and describe the Kieler Woche.

grammar.topic: festivals; an/zu + festival; wenn for yearly routines
grammar.point: Festival names go without an article: an Weihnachten, zu Ostern, an Silvester. For things you do every year you use wenn: the verb goes to the end of the wenn clause, then the main clause starts with its verb: Wenn Weihnachten ist, schmücken wir die Wohnung.
grammar.oneLine: Wenn Weihnachten ist, schmücken wir die Wohnung.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ist Weihnachten, wir schmücken die Wohnung.
mistake.right: Wenn Weihnachten ist, schmücken wir die Wohnung.
mistake.why: In the wenn clause the verb goes to the end (ist). After the comma the main clause starts with its verb (schmücken), then the subject.

terms.meaning: a special day or week that people celebrate every year: das Fest
a day when most people do not work: der Feiertag
something you do again and again, for example every year

cards.title: Before we start: a year full of festivals
cards.body: Since A1 you know the months and the seasons: Im Dezember ist es kalt. Today you fill that year with its big festivals: Silvester, Karneval, Ostern and Weihnachten. You learn the wish for each one, what people do, and you use wenn for things that happen every year. At the end you visit a big summer festival in the north.
steps: You already know: the months, the seasons, wenn for things that happen again and again, and sich freuen auf.
New today: the names of the festivals, their wishes, an or zu Weihnachten, and festival verbs like schmücken and anstoßen.
By the end you can: say when a festival is, what you do then, and how you feel about it.

examples.why: New today: the name of a festival.

examples.de: Wenn Weihnachten ist, schmücken wir die Wohnung.
examples.en: When it is Christmas, we decorate the flat.
examples.why: New today: wenn for a yearly routine.

cards.more: Think of the year as a calendar on the wall. You already know the months on it. Today you write the big festivals into that calendar, and next to each one a short wish, like a sticker: Guten Rutsch! for New Year, Frohe Ostern! for Easter, Frohe Weihnachten! for Christmas. Then you say what you do on that day. Because a festival comes back every year, the word wenn from lesson 5 fits perfectly.

cards.title: The festival year: Silvester, Karneval, Ostern, Weihnachten
cards.body: Silvester is the 31st of December, the last evening of the year. Karneval is in February, with costumes and parades. Ostern is in spring, Weihnachten is in December. A public holiday is der Feiertag: shops and offices are closed. Each festival has its own wish. Learn the wish as one block.
cards.lead: You know the months and seasons from A1. Now you put the big German festivals into that year and learn the short wish that belongs to each one.

examples.en: New Year’s Eve is on the 31st of December.

deeper.text: Weihnachten and Ostern are really plural words. That is why the wishes are Frohe Weihnachten! and Frohe Ostern! with -e: they are fixed blocks, so you do not need to build them. In a normal sentence you use the festival names without an article: Weihnachten ist im Dezember. Silvester works the same way.

example.de: Silvester feiern wir mit Freunden.
example.en: We celebrate New Year’s Eve with friends.

cards.more: Picture four stickers on your calendar. On the 31st of December: Silvester, and you say Guten Rutsch! (literally a good slide into the new year). In February: Karneval, with costumes; in Cologne people shout Alaaf!, in Mainz Helau! In spring: Ostern, Frohe Ostern! In December: Weihnachten, Frohe Weihnachten! A Feiertag is any day when most people do not work, for example Christmas Day or Easter Monday.

cards.title: an Weihnachten, zu Ostern: saying when
cards.body: To say when something happens, put an or zu before the festival: an Weihnachten, zu Ostern, an Silvester. There is no article. In the north people often say zu, in the south an; both are correct. For a normal holiday you use am, as with days: am Feiertag, am Sonntag.
cards.lead: Now you have the names of the festivals. To say when you do something, you need one little word before the festival name: an or zu.

examples.de: An Weihnachten sind wir bei meiner Oma.
examples.en: At Christmas we are at my grandma’s.

examples.de: Zu Ostern fahren Mira und Leon nach Hause.
examples.en: At Easter Mira and Leon go home.

examples.de: Am Feiertag sind die Geschäfte zu.
examples.en: On the public holiday the shops are closed.

deeper.text: Neujahr is the 1st of January, the first day of the new year. It works like the festivals: an Neujahr, with no article. So the night is an Silvester and the next morning is an Neujahr. Many people sleep long an Neujahr, because they celebrate until late an Silvester.

example.de: An Neujahr schlafen wir lange.
example.en: On New Year’s Day we sleep long.

cards.more: With days you say am: am Montag, am Feiertag. With the festival names you say an or zu and nothing else: an Weihnachten, zu Ostern, an Silvester. A common mistake is to add an article: an der Weihnachten is wrong, the right form is an Weihnachten. If you are not sure whether to use an or zu, just pick one: everybody understands both, and both are good German.

cards.title: What people do: schmücken, Kerzen, Feuerwerk, anstoßen
cards.body: Festivals have their own actions. Before Weihnachten people schmücken (decorate) the flat and put Kerzen (candles) on the table. An Silvester there is Feuerwerk at midnight, and people anstoßen: they clink glasses, often with Sekt. Anstoßen is separable: Wir stoßen an.
cards.lead: You can now say when a festival is. This card gives you the verbs and things that show what people actually do on those days.

examples.de: Mira stellt Kerzen auf den Tisch.
examples.en: Mira puts candles on the table.

examples.de: Um Mitternacht stoßen wir mit Sekt an.
examples.en: At midnight we clink glasses with sparkling wine.

deeper.text: In the Perfekt both verbs take haben. Anstoßen is separable, so ge- goes in the middle: angestoßen. Schmücken is regular: geschmückt. Anstoßen also changes its vowel with er, sie and es, like laufen: Ben stößt mit Anna an. In the ich and wir forms the vowel stays: ich stoße an.

example.de: An Silvester haben wir um Mitternacht angestoßen.
example.en: On New Year’s Eve we clinked glasses at midnight.

cards.more: Picture the flat on the 24th of December: Mira hangs stars on the window, Leon puts candles on the table. They schmücken the flat. Now picture the 31st of December: at midnight there are fireworks in the sky, and everyone lifts a glass. The glasses touch with a little clink: that is anstoßen. Many people drink Sekt then, but juice is fine too. Remember that an goes to the end: Wir stoßen an.

rows: die Wohnung schmücken, Kerzen auf den Tisch stellen
Eier suchen, mit der Familie essen

cards.title: Wenn Weihnachten ist, …: yearly routines with wenn
cards.body: In lesson 5 you used wenn for things that happen again and again. A festival comes back every year, so wenn fits well: Wenn Weihnachten ist, schmücken wir die Wohnung. In the wenn clause the verb goes to the end. Then the main clause starts with its verb.
cards.lead: You have the festival verbs. Now you join them with wenn from lessons 4 and 5, to say what you always do when a festival comes.

examples.de: Wenn Silvester ist, stoßen wir um Mitternacht an.
examples.en: When it is New Year’s Eve, we clink glasses at midnight.

examples.de: Immer wenn Karneval ist, feiert Anna in Köln.
examples.en: Whenever it is carnival, Anna celebrates in Cologne.

examples.de: Wenn Ostern ist, besucht Leon seine Eltern.
examples.en: When it is Easter, Leon visits his parents.

deeper.text: The wenn clause can also come second. Then the main clause has its normal order, and the wenn clause closes the sentence with its verb at the very end: Wir essen viel, wenn Weihnachten ist. Both orders mean the same. Start with wenn when you want the festival to be the first thing your listener hears.

example.de: Wir essen viel, wenn Weihnachten ist.
example.en: We eat a lot when it is Christmas.

cards.more: Think of two boxes. The first box is the wenn clause: Wenn Weihnachten ist. Its verb, ist, sits at the end of the box. After the comma comes the second box, and it opens with its verb: schmücken wir die Wohnung. So in the middle of the sentence two verbs stand side by side: ist, schmücken. That verb, verb pattern is the sign that you built it right. Never put the subject first in the second box.
steps: Start with Wenn and the festival: Wenn Weihnachten
Put the verb at the end of the wenn clause, then a comma: … ist,
Start the main clause with its verb: schmücken
Then the subject and the rest: wir die Wohnung.

cards.title: Die Kieler Woche: a summer festival in the north
cards.body: Kiel is a city on the sea in the north of Germany. Every year in June there is the Kieler Woche: one week of ships, music, food and fireworks at the harbour. Very many visitors come. You can describe it with the comparisons from chapter 3: Die Kieler Woche ist größer als ein Stadtfest.
cards.lead: After winter festivals and Easter, here is a summer one. You describe it with what you already have: wenn, comparisons and festival words.

examples.de: Die Kieler Woche ist im Juni.
examples.en: The Kiel Week is in June.

examples.de: Am Hafen gibt es Musik und Schiffe.
examples.en: At the harbour there is music and there are ships.

examples.de: Die Kieler Woche ist größer als ein Stadtfest.
examples.en: The Kiel Week is bigger than a town festival.

deeper.text: Kieler comes from the city name Kiel plus -er. You can do this with many cities: Berlin, Berliner; Köln, Kölner; Hamburg, Hamburger. This -er word never changes its ending, whatever the article: die Kieler Woche, der Kölner Karneval, das Berliner Wetter. It works like a fixed label in front of the noun.

example.de: Wir fahren im Juni zur Kieler Woche.
example.en: We are going to the Kiel Week in June.

cards.more: Imagine a big harbour by the sea. For one week in June it is full of white sails, music stages and food stalls, and at night there are fireworks over the water. That is the Kieler Woche, one of the biggest summer festivals in the north. You need no new grammar to talk about it: Die Kieler Woche ist im Juni. Am Hafen gibt es Musik. Wenn die Kieler Woche ist, ist die Stadt voll.

rows: in Kiel, am Meer, im Norden

cards.title: Feelings at festivals: Ich freue mich auf Weihnachten
cards.body: Festivals bring feelings, and you already have the reflexive verbs for them. Before a festival: Ich freue mich auf Weihnachten. During it: Ich fühle mich wohl. After it: Wir erholen uns. Something you do not like: Frau Weber ärgert sich über das Feuerwerk.
cards.lead: You can now say when a festival is and what you do. This last card brings back the reflexive verbs of lessons 1 and 2, to say how a festival feels.

examples.en: I am looking forward to Christmas.

examples.de: An Silvester ärgert sich Frau Weber über das Feuerwerk.
examples.en: On New Year’s Eve Frau Weber gets annoyed about the fireworks.
After Christmas we have a rest.

deeper.text: Remember the difference between auf and über with sich freuen. Sich freuen auf is for something that is still coming: Ich freue mich auf Weihnachten. Sich freuen über is for something that is already here: when you open a present, Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. The festival is the same, only the time changes.

example.de: Leon freut sich über die Kerze.
example.en: Leon is happy about the candle.

cards.more: A festival has three parts in time. Before it, you are looking forward: sich freuen auf. During it, you feel good or bad: sich wohlfühlen, sich ärgern über. After it, you are tired and you rest: sich erholen. If you remember those three steps, you always know which reflexive verb to take. And do not forget the little word mich, dich or sich: Ich freue mich, never just Ich freue.
